title: Power and First Offers
description: The party with more power—stronger alternatives, higher status, more information—is more likely to open assertively and capture value.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: The party with more power—stronger alternatives, higher status, more information—is more likely to open assertively and capture value.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A vendor with a unique product opens with 'Our price is $120,000. We don't negotiate on that.'
A job seeker with rare skills states, 'My expectation is $210,000 base. I'm not exploring below that.' He does not flinch.

sections.title: Typical Power Moves
content: Naming a first offer that is just inside the edge of realistic.
Using data or third-party validation to support the number.

sections.title: Warning Signs You Are Losing Power
content: You find yourself mentally justifying their number.
You ask 'Can you give me a small discount?' rather than resetting the anchor.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
sections.content: Boost your power perception before the negotiation. Do research to find a comparable deal, get a competing offer, or add value they can't easily replace. Even a single additional option shifts your internal posture.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Power is perceived as much as it is real. Walk in as if you have options—and make sure you actually do.
